question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Ace in the hole
option_1: To create noisy disturbances so that competitors are unable to work.
option_2: A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time.
option_3: To attempt to do the impossible.
option_4: To suffer an injury on the lower body.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Ace in the hole" means a hidden advantage or resource that is kept in reserve until it is needed, especially to turn a situation to one's favour. (गुप्त रखा गया लाभ, जरूरत पड़ने पर प्रयोग होने वाला)
◦ Example: The lawyer had an ace in the hole — a witness nobody knew about — which she produced only at the crucial moment of the trial.

• The phrase comes from card games such as stud poker, where a card ("ace") dealt face down ("in the hole") is hidden from other players and can be revealed at a decisive moment to win the game.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 describes creating noisy disturbances, which corresponds to idioms like "raise a hue and cry", not to "ace in the hole".

• Option 3 describes attempting the impossible, which corresponds to idioms like "reach for the moon" or "cry for the moon", not to "ace in the hole".

• Option 4 describes suffering a lower-body injury, which is unrelated to any standard idiomatic meaning of "ace in the hole".

NOTE

• Other idioms of hidden advantage/resource often asked in SSC: "A trump card" (a decisive resource kept for the right moment) and "A card up one's sleeve" (a hidden plan or resource).

• Do not confuse with "Achilles' heel", which means a person's hidden weakness, not an advantage.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Calibrate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gauge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Calibrate" means to check, adjust, or determine precisely the graduations of a measuring instrument, or to measure/assess something carefully against a standard. (किसी उपकरण को सही मापदंड के अनुसार जांचना/समायोजित करना)
◦ Example: The scientists had to calibrate the thermometer before using it for the experiment.

• "Gauge", as a verb, means to measure or determine precisely, or to estimate/judge, which closely matches the sense of "calibrate" — both involve precise measurement or assessment against a standard.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Gauze" means a thin, light, semi-transparent fabric (often used for bandages) — a similar-sounding word confused with "gauge" but with a completely different meaning.

• Option 2: "Assail" means to attack someone or something violently, or to criticise strongly — unrelated to measurement.

• Option 4: "Affront" means an action or remark that causes outrage or offence; an insult — unrelated to measurement.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the near-homophones "gauge" (to measure) and "gouge" (to cut/scoop out roughly, or to overcharge).

• Related words: calibration (noun), calibrated (adjective/past participle), often used in scientific and technical contexts (e.g., calibrating instruments, scales, or exam standards).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
The social ______ is going to meet with all of us tomorrow with the plans so we can make a decision.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. worker.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "social worker" is a person whose job is to help individuals, families, or communities with problems, provide guidance, and organise welfare-related plans. (समाज सेवक/सामाजिक कार्यकर्ता)
◦ Example: The social worker visited the village to discuss the new welfare scheme with the residents.

• The sentence states that this person "is going to meet with all of us tomorrow with the plans so we can make a decision" — this fits a social worker's role of organising and discussing plans with a group, which none of the other options logically support.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "army" does not collocate meaningfully with "social" in this context, and an army does not typically hold planning meetings of this personal nature.

• Option 3: "toddler" refers to a very young child, who would not be meeting people to discuss plans and make decisions.

• Option 4: "labour" means work/workforce in general and does not fit as a person coming to meet with "us" about plans; it is also not idiomatically paired with "social" in the way "social worker" is.

NOTE

• Common compound-noun pairings tested in SSC vocabulary questions: social worker, social work, social service, social security — note that "social" combines naturally with "worker" but not with the other given words.

• Do not confuse "social worker" (a welfare professional) with "socialite" (a person prominent in fashionable society).

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
He has been / told many a times to / mind his manners.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. told many a times to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "many a times".

• Rule — "Many a + singular noun": The expression "many a" is always followed by a singular countable noun, even though the meaning is plural. The correct form here is "many a time", not "many a times".
◦ Example: I have told him many a time to be careful. (correct)
◦ Incorrect: I have told him many a times to be careful.

• Applying the rule: "told many a times to" must be corrected to "told many a time to".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because there clearly is a grammatical error in the sentence, in the segment discussed above.

• Option 2: "He has been" is grammatically correct — it correctly sets up the passive structure "has been told", using the auxiliary correctly.

• Option 4: "mind his manners." is grammatically correct — "mind" is correctly used as an infinitive-of-purpose verb ("told...to mind his manners").

NOTE

• Alternative correct forms with the same meaning: "told many times" or "told time and again" (both plural constructions, without "a").

• "Many a" always takes a singular verb too: "Many a man has failed" (not "have failed"), since "many a" grammatically treats the noun as singular.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
In humans, lack of sleep leads to ______ memory and reduced cognitive abilities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. impaired.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Impaired" means weakened, damaged, or made less effective in function. (क्षतिग्रस्त/कमजोर हुआ)
◦ Example: Lack of sleep is known to cause impaired judgement and slower reaction times.

• The sentence discusses a negative consequence of lack of sleep — "reduced cognitive abilities" — so the blank must also describe something negative happening to memory; "impaired memory" (i.e., weakened memory) fits this logically and is a standard collocation in medical/psychological writing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "attended" means "given attention to" or "looked after" — it does not make sense with "memory" in a negative context like this.

• Option 3: "thankless" means "not likely to be appreciated" (as in "a thankless task") — it cannot logically describe "memory".

• Option 4: "witnessed" means "seen personally" — memory cannot be described as "witnessed" in this context.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "impaired": impaired vision, impaired hearing, impaired judgement, impaired memory, impaired mobility — all describe a reduced or damaged ability/function.

• Related word: "impairment" (noun) — e.g., "visual impairment", "hearing impairment".

question:
The given sentence is in active voice. Change the voice of the sentence. Select the correct option from the sentences given in options.
The story explores the conflicting range of human emotions.
option_1: The conflicting range of human emotions had explored by the story.
option_2: The conflicting range of human emotions did explored by the story.
option_3: The conflicting range of human emotions is explored by the story.
option_4: The conflicting range of human emotions has explored by the story.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The conflicting range of human emotions is explored by the story.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The story explores the conflicting range of human emotions" is in the Simple Present Tense (Subject + V1(s/es) + Object).

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the conflicting range of human emotions" becomes the subject of the passive sentence; since "range" (the head noun) is singular, the auxiliary used is "is"; the verb "explores" becomes the past participle "explored"; and "the story" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: The conflicting range of human emotions is explored by the story.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "had explored" without an auxiliary "been" is not a valid passive form at all, and it wrongly suggests the Past Perfect Tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "did explored" is grammatically invalid — the auxiliary "did" must be followed by the base form (V1), and in any case this does not form a correct passive construction.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has explored" without "been" is not a passive form; a correct Present Perfect passive would require "has been explored".

NOTE

• Passive voice always requires a form of "be" (is/am/are/was/were/being/been) + past participle (V3); a bare past-participle verb (without any form of "be") never forms a valid passive.

• The subject-verb agreement in the passive sentence is governed by the new subject (the former object) — here "range" is singular, so "is" (not "are") is used, despite "emotions" being plural elsewhere in the phrase.

question:
Some parts of one or more sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
At Paris, just after dark
A. of meditation and a meerschaum, in company
B. one gusty evening in the autumn
C. of 18, I was enjoying the twofold luxury
D. with my friend Auguste Dupin, in his little back library
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BCAD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• To solve rearrangement questions, identify the part that logically continues from the fixed opening line, and trace the sentence to a grammatically complete and meaningful whole.

• The fixed opening is "At Paris, just after dark,", which needs a time expression to continue — this is provided by B ("one gusty evening in the autumn"), immediately followed by the specific year in C ("of 18, I was enjoying the twofold luxury").

• The word "twofold luxury" in C needs to be explained by what the two things are — this is given in A ("of meditation and a meerschaum, in company"), which is then completed by D ("with my friend Auguste Dupin, in his little back library"), specifying whose company.

• Reading the parts in the order B–C–A–D gives: "At Paris, just after dark, one gusty evening in the autumn of 18, I was enjoying the twofold luxury of meditation and a meerschaum, in company with my friend Auguste Dupin, in his little back library" — a complete, meaningful, grammatically correct sentence (the opening of Edgar Allan Poe's "The Purloined Letter").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (CDBA) is incorrect because it places C ("of 18, I was enjoying...") directly after the fixed opening, which is grammatically disconnected without a time phrase like B first.

• Option 2 (ADBC) is incorrect because it starts with A ("of meditation..."), which cannot logically or grammatically follow "At Paris, just after dark" directly.

• Option 4 (DCBA) is incorrect because it begins with D ("with my friend Auguste Dupin..."), which cannot meaningfully follow the fixed opening line.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions, always look for grammatical connectors (prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions) and logical continuity (a phrase that needs a preceding or following element to make sense) to fix the sequence.

• Reading the fully reconstructed sentence aloud is a reliable final check — if it reads smoothly and makes complete sense, the sequence is correct.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.
I just don't like the themes of todays music.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. todays music.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word "todays", which is a possessive form and must carry an apostrophe: "today's".

• Rule — Possessive apostrophe: A singular noun (including time-expressions like "today", "yesterday", "a day's", "a week's") forms its possessive by adding apostrophe + s ('s).
◦ Example: today's music, yesterday's news, a day's work.

• Applying the rule: "todays music" must be corrected to "today's music", since "music" belongs to/is associated with "today".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because there is a clear punctuation/possessive error in the sentence, as explained above.

• Option 2: "I just don't" is correct — the contraction "don't" is properly formed and used.

• Option 3: "like the themes of" is grammatically correct with no error.

NOTE

• Time-expression possessives frequently tested in SSC: today's, yesterday's, tomorrow's, a moment's (notice), a day's (work), in two years' (time).

• Do not confuse the possessive "today's" with a simple plural, which never takes an apostrophe.

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given group of words.
A man who is womanish in his habits
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Effeminate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Effeminate" means a man who has qualities, habits, or mannerisms that are traditionally associated with women; womanish in behaviour. (स्त्रैण, जनाना स्वभाव वाला)
◦ Example: His effeminate mannerisms often drew comments from his classmates.

• The given phrase "A man who is womanish in his habits" is a direct definition of this word, making it the correct one-word substitution.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Indictment" (अभियोग): A formal charge or accusation of a serious crime.

• Option 3: "Hooch" (अवैध शराब): Illegally distilled or smuggled alcoholic liquor.

• Option 4: "Infidel" (काफ़िर/अधर्मी): A person who does not believe in a particular religion, especially one who does not believe in the religion considered to be the true one.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often confused with "effeminate": "misogynist" (one who hates women), "feminist" (one who advocates women's rights), "philanderer" (a man who has many casual affairs with women).

• "Effeminate" is used only for describing a man's manner; it is not applied to describe a woman.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. more stringent mobility control and physical distancing policies
Q. East Asian governments (except for Japan) implemented
R. as well as more comprehensive testing, tracing
S. and isolation policies since the early stages
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. QPRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must begin with a subject and a verb to introduce the action — this is provided by Q ("East Asian governments (except for Japan) implemented"), which needs an object to complete the verb "implemented".

• The object of "implemented" is given in P ("more stringent mobility control and physical distancing policies"), which is then extended by R ("as well as more comprehensive testing, tracing"), adding a further set of policies using the connector "as well as".

• R is completed by S ("and isolation policies since the early stages"), which finishes the list ("testing, tracing, and isolation policies") and adds the time reference "since the early stages".

• Reading the parts in the order Q–P–R–S gives: "East Asian governments (except for Japan) implemented more stringent mobility control and physical distancing policies as well as more comprehensive testing, tracing and isolation policies since the early stages" — a complete, meaningful, grammatically correct sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PSRQ) is incorrect because it starts with P, which requires a preceding subject-verb ("governments implemented") to make grammatical sense.

• Option 3 (PRSQ) is incorrect for the same reason — starting with the object P without the subject-verb Q leaves the sentence without a clear subject.

• Option 4 (QSPR) is incorrect because it places S ("and isolation policies since the early stages") immediately after Q, which breaks the logical listing of "testing, tracing and isolation policies" and leaves "policies" dangling without its main noun phrase P.

NOTE

• In rearrangement questions with parallel listed items (here: "testing, tracing, and isolation"), look for words like "as well as," "and," "along with" to correctly link the list in sequence.

• Always identify the part containing the main subject + finite verb first — it is very often (though not always) the correct starting part of the sentence.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Over and above
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In addition to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Over and above" means besides; in addition to; apart from what has already been mentioned. (के अतिरिक्त/इसके अलावा)
◦ Example: Over and above his salary, he receives a generous travel allowance.

• The idiom is typically used to introduce something extra that supplements what has already been stated, which matches the meaning "in addition to".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Above all" means "most importantly of all" — used to emphasise the most significant point, not to add something extra.

• Option 2: "To sum up the conversation" means to summarise — unrelated to the meaning of "over and above".

• Option 4: "Highest rank" describes a position/status and is unrelated to the idiomatic meaning of addition.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of addition often tested in SSC: "In addition to," "Apart from," "Not to mention," "Let alone" (used differently, in a negative sense).

• Do not confuse "Over and above" (in addition to) with "Over and done with" (completely finished).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
In this engineering design project you will learn how to build an infinity mirror, with built-in lights that make the mirror look like a deep ______ with no end.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. tunnel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "tunnel" is a long underground or enclosed passage, and the phrase "a deep tunnel with no end" is a common visual description of an endless receding passage of light and reflections — exactly the effect an infinity mirror creates. (सुरंग)
◦ Example: Looking into the infinity mirror felt like staring down a deep tunnel with no end.

• The context — "built-in lights that make the mirror look like a deep ______ with no end" — requires a word denoting a long, deep, enclosed passage, which only "tunnel" provides among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "lodge" means a small house or a temporary place to stay — it does not describe a deep, receding visual passage.

• Option 3: "funeral" refers to a ceremony held after a person's death — completely unrelated in meaning to the visual described.

• Option 4: "signal" refers to a sign or indication, not a deep enclosed passage — it does not fit the visual description at all.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "tunnel": tunnel vision (a narrow way of thinking), light at the end of the tunnel (hope after a difficult period), wind tunnel (a testing apparatus).

• The word tested here relies on contextual/descriptive vocabulary rather than grammar — always visualise the scenario described in fill-in-the-blank vocabulary questions to identify the best fit.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Book giving information about everything
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Encyclopedia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Encyclopedia" is a book or set of books giving information on many subjects or on many aspects of one subject, typically arranged alphabetically. (विश्वकोश)
◦ Example: She looked up the topic of volcanoes in the encyclopedia.

• The given phrase "Book giving information about everything" directly matches this definition, since an encyclopedia is compiled precisely to provide broad general knowledge across subjects.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Dictionary" (शब्दकोश): A book that lists words and gives their meanings, pronunciations, and usage — not general information about everything.

• Option 3: "Phonebook" (दूरभाष निर्देशिका): A book listing telephone numbers and addresses of people/organisations.

• Option 4: "Thesis" (शोध प्रबंध): A long, detailed piece of writing (based on research) submitted as part of a university degree.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often confused: "Thesaurus" (a book of synonyms and antonyms), "Almanac" (a book/table listing dates, astronomical/weather information for a year), "Atlas" (a book of maps).

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
WHIMSICAL
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. FUNNY.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Whimsical" means playfully quaint, fanciful, or unpredictable in an amusing or light-hearted way. (सनकी/विचित्र किन्तु मनोरंजक)
◦ Example: The story had a whimsical charm, with talking animals and floating houses.

• Among the given options, "FUNNY" is closest in spirit to "whimsical", since both describe something amusing, playful, or light-heartedly unusual, whereas the other options describe entirely unrelated qualities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "WEAK" means lacking physical or other strength — unrelated to playfulness or fancifulness.

• Option 2: "RESPECTFUL" means showing deference or esteem towards someone — unrelated to "whimsical".

• Option 3: "HUMILIATED" means made to feel ashamed or foolish — opposite in tone to the light-hearted sense of "whimsical".

NOTE

• Words associated with "whimsical": fanciful, capricious, quirky, playful, eccentric.

• Do not confuse "whimsical" (playfully fanciful) with "capricious" (given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behaviour, often with a more negative connotation of unreliability).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Instigate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Raise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Instigate" means to bring about or initiate an action by incitement; to stir up or provoke (an event, feeling, or action). (भड़काना/उकसाना)
◦ Example: The rumours were enough to instigate a riot in the town.

• "Raise", in the sense of stirring up or bringing about something (e.g., "to raise a rebellion," "to raise an alarm"), closely matches the sense of provoking or initiating something, which is the core meaning of "instigate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Deterrence" means the action of discouraging an action through fear of the consequences — the opposite sense of provoking something.

• Option 2: "Settle" means to resolve a matter or come to rest — the opposite of stirring something up.

• Option 4: "Complaisance" means a willingness to please others; agreeable compliance — unrelated to provoking or initiating.

NOTE

• Words with meanings close to "instigate": incite, provoke, foment, stir up, goad.

• Related noun form: "instigation" (e.g., "he acted at the instigation of his friend"); related agent noun: "instigator" (the person who provokes an action).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Inept
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Competent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Inept" means having or showing no skill; clumsy or unskillful; not suited to the purpose. (अक्षम/अयोग्य)
◦ Example: His inept handling of the negotiations cost the company an important client.

• "Competent" means having the necessary ability, skill, or knowledge to do something successfully, which is the direct opposite of being unskilled or clumsy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Wanting" means lacking or deficient (e.g., "found wanting") — this is close in meaning to "inept" rather than opposite to it.

• Option 3: "Barred" means prohibited or excluded — unrelated to skill or competence.

• Option 4: "Callow" means inexperienced and immature — similar in sense to "inept" (lacking maturity/skill), not opposite to it.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "inept": clumsy, incompetent, unskilful, bungling, maladroit.

• Antonyms of "inept" other than "competent": skilful, adept, proficient, capable.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Frighter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Freighter" — a large ship or aircraft used for transporting goods.
◦ Example: The freighter carried containers of machinery across the Pacific Ocean.

• Spelling key: FREIGHT + ER. Note the "ei" combination in "freight" (as in "eight", "weight", "neighbour") — the given word "Frighter" incorrectly drops the "e" after "fr" and misspells the base word "freight" as "fright".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Practical" is correctly spelled — an adjective meaning relating to practice or action rather than theory.

• Option 2: "Glowing" is correctly spelled — the present participle of "glow".

• Option 3: "Released" is correctly spelled — the past tense of "release".

NOTE

• Other "-eigh-" words with the same tricky vowel combination: weight, eight, neighbour, sleigh, weigh.

• Do not confuse "freighter" (a cargo ship, from "freight") with "fighter" (one who fights) — the two look superficially similar when misspelled.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: The joy definitely lies in cooking for others.
option_2: The joy definitely lyes in cooking for others.
option_3: The joy defintely lies in cooking for others.
option_4: The joy definitely lies in cokking for others.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The joy definitely lies in cooking for others.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 1 — "definitely," "lies," and "cooking" — is spelled correctly, making the sentence free of any spelling error.

• Spelling keys to remember: "definitely" contains "finite" within it (de-FINITE-ly) — a common memory aid; "lies" (present tense of "to lie," meaning to be located) is spelled with "ie", not "ye"; "cooking" has a double "o" and a single "k".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "lyes" is misspelled; the correct spelling is "lies".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "defintely" is misspelled; the correct spelling is "definitely" (the "i" after "fin" is missing).

• Option 4 is incorrect because "cokking" is misspelled; the correct spelling is "cooking" (double "o", single "k").

NOTE

• Common SSC spelling traps: definitely (not "definately"), separate (not "seperate"), occurred (double "c", double "r"), necessary (one "c", two "s").

• For homophone-type errors like "lies/lyes", always check the word functions correctly with its intended meaning in the sentence.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A lover of oneself, of one's advancement
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Egoist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Egoist" is a person who is excessively concerned with themselves, their own interests and advancement; a self-centred person. (स्वार्थी/अहंवादी)
◦ Example: He was such an egoist that he only ever spoke about his own achievements.

• The given phrase "A lover of oneself, of one's advancement" directly describes a person driven by self-interest and self-promotion, which is the precise meaning of "egoist".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Philistine" (अरसिक/असंस्कृत व्यक्ति): A person who is hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts.

• Option 2: "Mercenary" (भाड़े का सैनिक/स्वार्थ के लिए काम करने वाला): A professional soldier hired to serve in a foreign army; also, a person primarily motivated by monetary gain.

• Option 3: "Cynic" (निंदक/संशयवादी): A person who believes people are motivated purely by self-interest and distrusts sincerity or goodness in others.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Egoist" (self-centred person) with "Egotist" (a person who talks about themselves excessively/boastfully) — the two are closely related but subtly distinct in usage.

• Related one-word substitution: "Altruist" — the opposite concept, a person who is unselfishly concerned for the welfare of others.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
Gloria said, “His relatives are landing tomorrow.”
option_1: Gloria said that his relatives are landing the next day.
option_2: Gloria said that his relatives were landing the previous day.
option_3: Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.
option_4: Gloria said that his relatives have been landing the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reported speech is in the Present Continuous Tense ("are landing"), and the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, so the tense of the reported speech must shift back.

• Rule — Present Continuous → Past Continuous in narration: When the reporting verb is in the past tense, "is/am/are + V-ing" changes to "was/were + V-ing".

• Rule — change of time expression: The word "tomorrow" in direct speech changes to "the next day" (or "the following day") in indirect speech.

• Applying both rules: "are landing" → "were landing" (plural subject "relatives", so "were"); "tomorrow" → "the next day". This gives: Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it retains "are landing" unchanged — the tense must shift to past continuous since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it wrongly changes "tomorrow" to "the previous day", which would mean the day before, not the day after, reversing the intended meaning; "tomorrow" must become "the next day".

• Option 4 is incorrect because it uses "have been landing" (Present Perfect Continuous), which is not the correct tense-shift of the Present Continuous Tense.

NOTE

• Common time-expression changes in narration: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day/the day before; last night → the previous night; here → there.

• "This/these" generally change to "that/those" in indirect speech as well, following the same logic of shifting reference away from the moment of speaking.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

People may seek fashion as part of (1) ______ they are and may want to be a fashion lover, which may lead them to spend more time (2) ______ out the latest fashion trends and more money than others on fashion products. We all know the good feeling that goes (3) ______ walking out of a store with a new shade of lipstick or after ordering a killer pair of boots online. They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. who.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "as part of who they are" is a common idiomatic expression referring to a person's identity — that is, the qualities and characteristics that define who a person fundamentally is.

• Rule: The relative/interrogative pronoun "who" is used to introduce a noun clause referring to a person's identity, and functions here as the subject of the embedded clause "they are ___", completing the sense "part of who they are" (part of their identity).

• Applying the rule: "People may seek fashion as part of who they are" means people may see fashion choices as an expression of their own identity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "which" is used for things, not for expressing personal identity in this fixed idiomatic sense; "part of which they are" does not make sense here.

• Option 2: "whom" is the objective form of "who" and is not used as the subject of the embedded clause "___ they are"; it would be grammatically incorrect here.

• Option 3: "whose" is a possessive pronoun ("belonging to whom") and does not fit the sentence structure, which requires a subject pronoun for the clause "they are".

NOTE

• The fixed phrase "part of who [subject] is/are" is commonly used in modern English to talk about personal identity, e.g., "Music is part of who I am."

• Distinguish carefully between who (subject), whom (object), and whose (possession) when filling blanks involving personal pronouns in noun clauses.

They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. seeking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal expression "seeking out" means to search for and find something, especially deliberately and persistently.

• The sentence describes people who "spend more time ___ out the latest fashion trends" — this matches the meaning of actively searching for and discovering fashion trends, i.e., "seeking out".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "freaking" — "freaking out" means becoming very anxious, excited, or frightened; it does not fit the context of researching fashion trends.

• Option 3: "doing" — "doing out" is not a standard English phrasal verb and does not fit the context.

• Option 4: "making" — "making out" typically means to manage/succeed, or to perceive something with difficulty, or informally to kiss; none of these fit the context of spending time researching fashion trends.

NOTE

• Common phrasal verbs with "out" tested in SSC: seek out (search for), find out (discover), figure out (understand), sort out (resolve), point out (indicate).

• Only "seeking out" logically collocates with "the latest fashion trends" as something people actively search for.

We all know the good feeling that goes (3) ______ walking out of a store with a new shade of lipstick or after ordering a killer pair of boots online. They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. along with.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "goes along with" means accompanies or occurs together with.

• The sentence states "the good feeling that goes ___ walking out of a store with a new shade of lipstick" — this describes a feeling that accompanies (occurs together with) the act of walking out of the store, which matches "along with".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "off in" is not a standard collocation with "goes" in this sense and does not fit grammatically.

• Option 2: "within" would suggest the feeling occurs inside the act itself in a spatial sense, which is not idiomatic English usage here; "goes within" is not a natural collocation.

• Option 3: "up in" does not form a meaningful or idiomatic phrase with "goes" in this context.

NOTE

• Common phrase: "goes along with" (accompanies, is consistent with) — e.g., "The responsibility that goes along with the job."

• Do not confuse "go along with" (to accompany/agree with) with "go along" (to proceed or make progress) — the presence of "with" changes the required following structure.

They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. backed up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "back up" means to support or confirm something with evidence.

• The sentence states "more than one scientific study has ___ its effectiveness" — this means multiple studies have provided supporting evidence for retail therapy's effectiveness, which matches "backed up".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "held back" means to restrain or hold something in check, or to withhold — this would mean the opposite of confirming effectiveness, so it does not fit.

• Option 2: "summed up" means to summarise briefly — a study cannot "sum up" its own effectiveness in this sense; the sentence requires a verb of confirmation/support.

• Option 4: "sold on" means to be convinced or enthusiastic about something ("sold on an idea") — it is typically used with a person as the subject who is convinced, not with a study as the subject confirming a fact; it does not fit the grammar here.

NOTE

• Common phrasal verbs with "up" expressing confirmation/support: back up (support with evidence), back (to support), confirm, corroborate, substantiate.

• "Backed up" is frequently used in academic and journalistic contexts to describe evidence supporting a claim, e.g., the claim is backed up by extensive research.

People may seek fashion as part of (1) ______ they are and may want to be a fashion lover, which may lead them to spend more time (2) ______ out the latest fashion trends and more money than others on fashion products. We all know the good feeling that goes (3) ______ walking out of a store with a new shade of lipstick or after ordering a killer pair of boots online. They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. or.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "or" is used to present alternatives — two or more different possible options between which a choice exists.

• The sentence states "whether it is being done online ___ in your favourite store" — this presents two alternative modes of shopping (online, or in a physical store), which requires the coordinating conjunction "or" to link the alternatives, especially following the correlative "whether".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "if" does not fit grammatically after "whether... online ___ in your favourite store", since "whether" already sets up a choice between alternatives, which needs "or", not "if".

• Option 2: "and" would incorrectly suggest both things happen simultaneously (online and in-store at once), rather than presenting them as alternative options, which contradicts the intended meaning.

• Option 4: "so" is a conjunction of result/consequence and does not fit the structure of presenting two alternative locations for shopping.

NOTE

• Rule — "whether...or": The correlative conjunction pair "whether...or" is used to present two (or more) alternatives, e.g., "Whether you like it or not, you must go."

• Do not confuse "whether" (introducing a choice/alternatives) with "weather" (atmospheric conditions) — a common homophone trap in SSC exams.
